era: Road to Rupture: The 2025 Trade War

events.title: Trump Invokes IEEPA, Imposes 25% Tariffs on Canada and Mexico
events.detail: President Trump signed executive orders under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act declaring a national emergency over fentanyl and migration, imposing 25% tariffs on most Canadian and Mexican goods and 10% on Canadian energy exports, effective March 4. It was the first time IEEPA had been used to justify tariffs.

sources.name: Wikipedia: 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada and Mexico

events.title: Canada Announces CA$155B in Retaliatory Tariffs
events.detail: Then-PM Justin Trudeau announced 25% retaliatory tariffs on CA$30 billion of US goods immediately, rising to CA$155 billion (US$107 billion) after three weeks if the US tariffs proceeded. Trudeau called the US justification 'completely bogus' and 'very dumb.'

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: Mark Carney Elected Liberal Leader, Becomes PM
events.detail: Former central banker Mark Carney won the Liberal Party leadership with 85.9% on the first ballot and was sworn in as Canada's Prime Minister on March 14, pledging to maintain retaliatory tariffs and diversify trade away from the United States.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: Ontario Slaps, Then Suspends, 25% Electricity Surcharge
events.detail: Premier Doug Ford imposed a 25% surcharge on electricity exports to Michigan, Minnesota and New York in response to US tariffs, then suspended it hours later after a 'productive conversation' with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The one-day surcharge raised roughly $260,000 before being pulled.

events.title: US Doubles Steel and Aluminum Tariffs to 50%
events.detail: Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum imports doubled from 25% to 50%, excluding the UK. Canada, the largest US supplier of both metals, warned the tariffs would make the American market 'essentially inaccessible' and threaten roughly 23,000 steel and 9,500 aluminum jobs.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: Canada Cancels Digital Services Tax to Resume Talks
events.detail: After Trump abruptly ended trade negotiations over Canada's pending Digital Service Tax targeting US tech firms, Carney announced the tax's cancellation, allowing bilateral talks to resume the next day.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: Ford's Anti-Tariff Ad Campaign Blows Up Talks
events.detail: Ontario Premier Doug Ford's $75 million ad campaign, featuring Ronald Reagan's 1987 warning against tariffs, prompted Trump to call the ads 'fraudulent' and terminate ongoing negotiations. The US responded two days later with an additional 10% tariff on Canadian goods.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: Canada Lifts Most Counter-Tariffs
events.detail: Effective September 1, Canada lifted nearly all retaliatory counter-tariffs on US goods, keeping measures only on steel, aluminum and automotive products — a de-escalation gesture that did not resolve the underlying dispute.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: Carney Declares 'Rupture' of Post-Cold War Order at Davos
events.detail: Addressing the World Economic Forum, PM Carney described a 'rupture' of the post-Cold War rules-based international order and called for middle powers to cooperate on trade diversification, foreshadowing the language that would define the tracker's namesake event.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: Canada Unveils Plan to Boost Non-US Trade and Investment
events.detail: Ottawa announced plans to expand non-US trade, strengthen interprovincial commerce, and increase domestic investment by CA$1 trillion over five years, part of a broader strategy to reduce dependence on the American market.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: Supreme Court Strikes Down IEEPA Tariffs in Learning Resources v. Trump
events.detail: In a 6-3 decision authored by Chief Justice Roberts, the Supreme Court ruled IEEPA does not authorize sweeping, open-ended tariffs, invalidating the central legal pillar of Trump's trade strategy. All IEEPA-based tariffs terminated at midnight February 24. The ruling left unresolved the fate of more than $166 billion already collected, sending the refund question back to the Court of International Trade.

events.title: Trump Pivots to Section 122 and Section 232 Authority
events.detail: Days after the IEEPA ruling, the administration proclaimed new tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 (a 15%-cap, 150-day emergency authority) and expanded Section 232 national-security tariffs on steel, aluminum, copper, furniture, cabinets, softwood lumber and buses, alongside a 10% Section 122 tariff on other exports — largely preserving the trade war's practical effect while resting on firmer legal ground.

events.title: Canada Enters Technical Recession
events.detail: Statistics Canada confirmed the economy contracted for a second consecutive quarter in Q1 2026, pushing Canada into a technical recession as tariffs, weak business investment and softer exports weighed on growth — a reversal from the resilience shown through most of 2025.

events.title: Carney Pledges Not to Weaponize Energy or Critical Minerals
events.detail: Ahead of the July joint review, PM Carney stated Canada would not use energy or critical minerals exports as 'leverage' in CUSMA negotiations, seeking to differentiate Ottawa's approach from more confrontational retaliatory options being debated domestically.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: USTR Proposes Additional 10% Tariff on Mexican Imports
events.detail: The USTR proposed an additional 10% tariff on Mexican goods outside USMCA coverage, which Mexico's Ministry of Economy immediately contested. President Sheinbaum called for sovereignty and a negotiated solution rather than retaliation.

events.title: USTR Implements 10% Forced-Labor Tariff on Mexican Goods
events.detail: USTR formally implemented Section 301 forced-labor tariffs on 60 economies following investigations into enforcement of forced-labor import bans, assigning Mexico a 10% rate effective July 24. USMCA-compliant Mexican goods remain exempt, but the action gave concrete legal effect to the additional 10% non-USMCA baseline USTR had floated on June 2 without a formal order.

events.title: USTR Greer: US Will Not Extend USMCA
events.detail: At the mandatory six-year joint review under Article 34.7, USTR Jamieson Greer announced the United States would not confirm intent to extend USMCA for a further 16-year term, citing 'shortcomings' in the deal and persistent trade deficits with Canada and Mexico. Canada and Mexico both backed extension. The decision triggers annual reviews under Article 34.7.4 until the agreement's scheduled July 1, 2036 expiry; existing tariff preferences, rules of origin, investment protections and dispute settlement remain operative in the meantime.

events.title: US-Mexico Bilateral Negotiating Round Opens in Mexico City
events.detail: Following the failed joint review, the US and Mexico began the first of several bilateral negotiating rounds in Mexico City, covering economic security, labor, agriculture, electronic payments, steel and aluminum, and automotive rules of origin, while Canada had not yet begun substantive text-based talks.

events.title: Trump Invokes Section 338 for First Time in 70+ Years
events.detail: Trump signed three proclamations under the long-dormant Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, imposing 50% tariffs on Canadian motor vehicles, alcohol, dairy and other goods effective August 19 — with no USMCA exemption, even for compliant goods. The move covered nearly $20 billion in annual Canadian imports across wine, hockey sticks, cement, electronics, furniture, lumber, clothing, footwear, toys, machinery and cosmetics.

events.title: Gordie Howe International Bridge Opens Amid Tariff Turmoil
events.detail: The long-delayed Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor and Detroit opened to traffic, adding capacity to a corridor that carries roughly 30% of Canada-US trade by truck and more than $274 million in trade daily — a symbol of deep continental integration opening just as tariff escalation threatened it.

events.title: Trump Threatens Tariffs Over Canadian Wildfire Smoke
events.detail: Trump threatened new tariffs in response to smoke from Canadian wildfires drifting into the United States, an unconventional escalation that Canadian officials dismissed as unrelated to trade policy but that underscored the volatility of the relationship heading into the Section 338 deadline.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: US-Mexico Wrap Third Round of USMCA Talks as New Tariffs Bite
events.detail: USTR Greer and Mexican Secretary of Economy Marcelo Ebrard concluded a third bilateral round in Washington, reporting 'constructive' progress on steel, aluminum and Asian-import substitution even as new Section 338 tariffs on Canada took effect in parallel. Mexico's own tariff exposure stayed largely capped near the pre-existing 10% baseline outside USMCA.

events.title: US and Mexico Set Fourth USMCA Round for September
events.detail: Greer and Ebrard directed negotiating teams to convene a fourth bilateral round in Washington in September 2026, with automotive content rules and regional rules of origin still unresolved — raising the prospect that a full agreement could slip into 2027.

events.title: Sheinbaum Publicly Rejects US Tariff Policy
events.detail: President Sheinbaum told reporters at her morning press conference, 'We haven't agreed with the tariffs... nor has virtually any other country, because we believe there are other mechanisms... to strengthen one economic region relative to another,' reiterating Mexico's preference for negotiation over confrontation while pushing back on US framing of the dispute.

events.title: Greer: Canada Must Drop Retaliation or Face New Tariffs
events.detail: Speaking at the Iowa State Fair, USTR Greer said Canada must scrap remaining retaliatory measures — including provincial bans on US alcohol sales — to avoid the Section 338 tariffs taking effect August 19. 'For us, this is not a trade war,' Greer said. 'If a country retaliates against us, we're obviously not going to tolerate that,' likening Canadian retaliation to Chinese trade tactics.

events.title: Trump Pauses 50% Tariffs for Three Days as Deal Nears
events.detail: Hours ahead of the August 19 effective date, Trump paused the 50% Section 338 tariffs on Canadian goods, citing progress toward a bilateral deal. Carney asked provincial premiers to begin restocking American alcohol on store shelves as a good-faith gesture.

events.title: Trump and Carney Announce 'Very Fair' Trade Deal
events.detail: Trump declared 'we've come to a deal with Canada,' saying it would eliminate tariffs on US farm exports to Canada and could lower US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos, while Canada lowers remaining retaliatory tariffs. Trump floated reviving the cancelled Keystone XL pipeline as part of the package. Carney was more measured, warning 'important work' remained and that the deal was 'subject to finalization of documents.'

events.title: Saskatchewan Premier: Threatened Tariffs 'Not Coming Into Effect'
events.detail: Premier Scott Moe confirmed the threatened 50% Section 338 tariffs on nearly CA$30 billion of Canadian goods would not take effect as negotiations with the Trump administration continued, providing the clearest provincial confirmation of the last-minute reprieve.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Timeline of the 2025–2026 US trade war with Canada

events.title: Carney Moves to Unwind Retaliation Ahead of Deal Signing
events.detail: As part of the deal package, PM Carney asked provincial premiers to restock American alcohol and drop 'Buy Canadian' procurement exclusions targeting US firms — the clearest sign yet that Ottawa intends to unwind its remaining retaliatory measures once a final agreement is signed. Ontario and British Columbia held out for firmer tariff commitments before complying; liquor bans remained lifted only in Saskatchewan and Alberta as of Aug 21.

events.title: LeBlanc: Dairy Supply Management Will Stay 'Entirely Intact' in Deal
events.detail: Canada-US Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told reporters after meeting USTR Greer in Washington that Canada's dairy supply-management system would remain 'entirely intact' in the emerging deal, addressing a top Canadian red line as talks continued past the Aug 19 tariff deadline.

events.title: LeBlanc, Greer Hold 3+ Hour Session, Call Deal 'Very Close'
events.detail: LeBlanc met Greer in Washington for a three-hour-plus negotiating session he described as 'long' and 'detailed,' after which he said the two sides were 'very close' to a final agreement. Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette, Canadian Ambassador Mark Wiseman and Carney's Chief of Staff Marc-André Blanchard also took part.

events.title: Mexico Pushes for Parity After Seeing US-Canada Draft Terms
events.detail: Bloomberg reported the tentative US-Canada deal — cutting steel and aluminum tariffs to 25% (under a roughly 4-million-metric-ton quota) and autos to a 15% headline rate before US-content deductions — caught Mexican officials off guard, prompting Mexico to press for comparable relief after three bilateral rounds since May produced no similar tariff reductions.

events.title: Deal Still Unsigned as Aug 22 Tariff Deadline Nears
events.detail: With the three-day pause on Section 338 tariffs set to expire at 12:01 a.m. ET Saturday, LeBlanc and Greer resumed talks in Washington Friday morning without a signed agreement in hand. Steel, aluminum and auto tariff cuts were reportedly close to final, but softwood lumber and agriculture remained unresolved; failure to close the deal in time would trigger the 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods including hockey sticks and wine.

events.title: Auto Parts Industry Warns Any Deal Must Cut Tariffs Below 6%
events.detail: Flavio Volpe, president of Canada's Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association and a Team Canada trade adviser, warned that a 10-15% auto tariff 'does not work for car makers or parts makers' and that any durable deal needed rates below the industry's roughly 6% profit margin — after six decades of near-zero tariffs under NAFTA and USMCA.

events.title: US-Canada Trade Talks Collapse Hours Before Tariff Deadline
events.detail: Negotiations in Washington broke down late Friday night, minutes before the 12:01am ET Saturday deadline, ending days of talks that Trump had called 'pretty much' a deal just hours earlier. PM Carney suspended negotiations and recalled Canada's negotiating team to Ottawa, saying the US had proposed new terms in recent days that were 'uneconomic, unfair and undermined the net benefits for Canada' — including restrictions on Canada's ability to pursue independent trade deals and provisions touching French-language subsidies and bilingual labeling. USTR Jamieson Greer countered that Canada 'declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week' and had walked back prior commitments, calling it 'a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States' and confirming no new talks were currently planned.

media.caption: US-Canada trade talks collapse hours before the Section 338 tariff deadline

events.title: 50% Tariffs Take Effect on $20B of Canadian Goods; Carney: 'We're at War'
events.detail: The Section 338 tariffs took legal effect at 12:01am ET Saturday after the deal collapsed, hitting roughly $20 billion (C$28 billion) of Canadian goods — about 5% of Canada's exports to the US — including electronics, plastics, wood, paper, dairy, alcohol, cement, clothing and hockey equipment. Energy, potash, fish, critical minerals and goods already under Section 232 national-security tariffs remained exempt. At a Saturday press conference, Carney said 'You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,' and separately called the US move 'a miscalculation,' while acknowledging the tariffs would raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians and also hit 'innocent' US companies and states.

media.caption: 50% Section 338 tariffs take effect on Canadian goods after talks collapse

events.title: Carney Announces Dollar-for-Dollar Retaliation Effective Sept 8
events.detail: Speaking in Ottawa, PM Carney announced Canada will match the new US tariffs 'dollar for dollar' with retaliatory measures on roughly $20 billion of American goods, targeting steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. The measures take effect 'the Tuesday after Labor Day' — September 8, 2026 — with a detailed list to follow in the coming days. Carney said 'America has changed' and the two countries would 'not return to our old relationship.'

media.caption: Carney announces Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs, effective Sept 8

events.title: Trump Tells Canada to 'Fall in Line,' Threatens 50% Tariffs on Autos, Trucks and Steel From Jan 1
events.detail: Trump posted on Truth Social that Canada must 'fall in line' or face consequences 'far WORSE' than the tariffs already in place, threatening new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, trucks, auto parts and steel effective January 1, 2027, and referring to Carney as 'Governor Carney.' Carney rejected the framing, saying an attitude 'that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States' was 'not something we're going to accept,' and that US trade demands showed Washington wanted to 'destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum.'

media.caption: Trump threatens 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, trucks and steel starting Jan 1, 2027

events.title: Ottawa Unveils Detailed Retaliation: 15-50% Tariffs on C$27.6B of US Goods Plus C$7.5B Worker Support
events.detail: Finance Minister Champagne, Industry Minister Joly, Jobs Minister Hajdu and AI Minister Solomon detailed Canada's Sept 8 retaliation package: a sliding scale of 15%, 25% and 50% tariffs covering roughly C$27.6 billion of US goods. The 50% tier hits steel, aluminum, furniture, clothing, perfumes, cosmetics, smartphones, dairy products, kitchenware, plywood, paper products, honey, doors, windows and cutlery; the 25% tier covers seafood, large kitchen appliances, cheese/curd products, carpets and textiles; 15% applies to air conditioners. Energy was excluded from the countermeasures. Ottawa paired the tariffs with a C$7.5 billion worker and business support package: temporary EI eligibility changes (C$3.5B, including a waived one-week waiting period and 20 extra weeks of benefits for long-tenured workers), a Regional Tariff Response Initiative (C$1.5B), a Business Development Bank liquidity program (C$500M), and a Canada Strong Diversification Fund (C$2B). Carney said Canada 'could not accept what the US had offered, nor could we give what they had asked.'

media.caption: Canada unveils detailed sliding-scale retaliatory tariffs on C$27.6B of US goods

events.title: Ford Letter Reveals Push to Target Tariffs at Eight Trump-Aligned States
events.detail: A letter from Ontario Premier Doug Ford to PM Carney, dated Aug 17 and reported Aug 23, called for 'additional retaliatory tariffs' targeting eight US states — Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Iowa, Missouri, Montana, Texas and Wisconsin — which Ford described as 'politically significant states to the current administration's base of support.' Carney's office said the PM had since met with premiers on the dollar-for-dollar countermeasures taking effect Sept 8, but did not adopt state-specific targeting; Carney said Canada would retaliate 'reluctantly,' noting some US businesses and states were 'innocent bystanders in a dispute they did not want.'

media.caption: Doug Ford's letter proposed targeting eight Trump-aligned US states with additional tariffs

events.title: Alberta's Current and Former Premiers Split Publicly Over Energy Leverage
events.detail: Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney said oil, gas and potash export taxes 'need to be on the table' as leverage against Washington and pressed Conservative MPs to publicly blame Trump for starting the trade war. Current Premier Danielle Smith rejected an energy export tax, warning 'no one wins a trade war' and that a 50% export tariff on the roughly 4 million barrels of oil Canada sells the US daily would risk losing the American customer 'entirely, if not forever,' costing jobs across Alberta, Ontario and Quebec. Smith cited $1.5 billion of Alberta exports facing US tariffs against $4.8 billion of Alberta goods exposed to Canada's own C$27.6 billion retaliation package, and called for 'doubling down' on diplomacy instead of further escalation.

media.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and former premier Jason Kenney publicly disagree over using energy exports as trade-war leverage

events.title: Trump Signs Executive Order Renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America' Amid Trade War
events.detail: President Trump signed an executive order on Aug 27, 2026 directing the Interior Department to work with the Board on Geographic Names over 30 days to redesignate Lake Ontario as 'Lake America'; the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) updated its database immediately, and Google Maps began showing 'Lake America' to US users, 'Lake Ontario' to Canadian users, and both names elsewhere. The move followed a Truth Social threat on Aug 25 and days of sparring with Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who had called Trump a 'loser' and a 'dictator.' Trump said Canadian officials 'haven't treated us well... they're nasty people.' PM Carney rejected the change, noting the Wendat-derived name predates both Canadian Confederation and US independence by centuries and vowing Canadians will call it 'Lake Ontario — then, now and always.' Seneca Nation President J. Conrad Seneca separately called for the order's rescission, citing the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua.

media.caption: Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America' amid the trade war with Canada

events.title: House Democrats Introduce 'Hands Off Our Great Lakes Act' to Nullify Lake Ontario Renaming
events.detail: On Aug 31, 2026, Reps. Joe Morelle (D-NY, lead sponsor), Debbie Dingell (D-MI) and Tim Kennedy (D-NY) introduced the 'Hands Off Our Great Lakes Act,' which would declare Trump's Aug 27 executive order renaming Lake Ontario 'no force or effect,' bar the president, the Interior Secretary and other federal officials from changing the official names of any of the five Great Lakes, and block federal funds from being used to implement the renaming. Morelle called the order 'ridiculous' and 'embarrassing,' saying 'no executive order, proclamation, or presidential temper tantrum' would change the lake's name. The bill lands amid broader Democratic criticism — Schumer called the renaming 'sad and pathetic,' Sanders and Schiff framed it as a distraction from affordability issues — even as the trade war's substantive stakes remain live ahead of Canada's Sept 8 retaliatory tariffs.

media.caption: Rep. Joe Morelle introduces the Hands Off Our Great Lakes Act to block Trump's Lake Ontario renaming

events.title: Ottawa Drops Seafood From Retaliation List, Adds Copper Wire and Charcoal
events.detail: Two days after unveiling its C$27.6 billion retaliation package, Canada's Department of Finance published a revised counter-tariff list dated Aug 26 that removed all 254 tariff lines covering fish and seafood (HS Chapter 3) — including Pacific and Atlantic salmon, swordfish, trout, tuna and sardines — that had been set for a 25% duty. The department said it made 'select adjustments to protect against broader economic harms, including removing seafood and fish products from our list of counter tariffs, while maintaining dollar for dollar and rate for rate response to US products.' Nine items were added at the 50% tier — wood charcoal, printed matter, gypsum board, glass containers and copper wire — cutting the total list from 874 to 629 tariff lines while the stated affected value stayed near C$27.6 billion. The Canadian Independent Fish Harvesters' Federation and Maine's congressional delegation both welcomed the reversal, citing an integrated, time-sensitive supply chain that crosses the border — nearly half of Maine's fall lobster catch is processed in New Brunswick.

media.caption: Canada removed fish and seafood products from its Sept 8 counter-tariff list after industry warnings about cross-border supply chain harm

events.title: Ford Unveils 'Lake Ontario. Now and Always' Sign on Grimsby Shoreline
events.detail: Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a 24-by-12-foot bilingual sign reading 'Lake Ontario. Now and Always' on the Lake Ontario shoreline near Grimsby, Ontario, three days after Trump's executive order directing federal agencies to redesignate the lake 'Lake America.' Wearing a Team Canada jersey, Ford said 'Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,' framing the display as part of Canada's broader posture of 'standing up for ourselves' amid the tariff dispute. The stunt followed PM Carney's own rejection of the renaming, which cited the Wendat-derived name's roughly 400-year history predating both Canadian Confederation and US independence.

media.caption: Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveils a giant 'Lake Ontario. Now and Always' sign near Grimsby in response to Trump's renaming order

events.title: Carney: US Wants to 'Wipe Out' Canadian Industries or Make Them Subsidiaries
events.detail: In remarks published Sept 1, 2026, PM Carney said the United States' negotiating posture aimed to either eliminate Canadian industries outright or convert them into subsidiaries of American firms, and that substantive trade talks could resume only once Washington stopped 'doing memes' and 'throwing shade' at Canada on social media. The comments came as the Liberals were separately confirmed to have swept all three federal byelections on Aug 31, restoring Carney's parliamentary majority, and as the Sept 8 retaliatory tariff deadline drew closer with no new negotiating session scheduled.

media.caption: PM Carney says US trade demands aim to 'wipe out' Canadian industries or turn them into subsidiaries

events.title: Sheinbaum: Mexico Among 'Best-Positioned' Countries, Pushing for Better Steel/Auto Terms
events.detail: At her Sept 3, 2026 morning press conference, President Sheinbaum said Mexico remained among the 'best-positioned' countries in trade with the US, noting most Mexican exports still enter duty-free under USMCA. She said her government was 'working very hard' to secure a better agreement on steel, aluminum and automobiles specifically, with Economy Secretary Ebrard making frequent trips to Washington ahead of the fourth bilateral round. Sheinbaum did not disclose new negotiating positions but expressed confidence a 'beneficial agreement' was achievable, maintaining Mexico's non-retaliation posture even as Canada's Sept 8 retaliatory tariffs approached.

media.caption: President Sheinbaum discusses steel, aluminum and auto tariff negotiations at her Sept 3 morning press conference

events.title: Lutnick Blames Canadian Politics for Talks Collapse; Carney Says US Moved Its Own Red Lines
events.detail: Speaking in Thunder Bay on Sept 3, 2026, PM Carney rejected US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's public claim that Canada had introduced 'crazy ideas' in the final hours of talks and walked away for domestic political reasons tied to Quebec's provincial election and Alberta's referendum. Carney called the claim wrong, saying 'I don't think, with all respect, appointed, unelected cabinet members in the United States are experts on Canadian politics.' Carney further said US negotiators had taken a 'take-it-or-leave-it' stance on several issues right up to the last hour before the Aug 21 collapse, then shifted position on some of those same points afterward — 'some of what they're saying now is different than what they were drawing the line on.' No new negotiating session was announced; Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs remained on track for Sept 8.

media.caption: Carney rejects Lutnick's claim that Canadian domestic politics caused the trade talks collapse

events.title: Trump Warns Carney Against Making Him 'The Enemy'
events.detail: Responding to the Sept 3 exchange with Lutnick, Trump posted on Truth Social that it was 'very good for Canadian Politicians like Prime Minister Carney to make President Donald J. Trump the enemy, until their Economy collapses, then it will prove to be very bad for Politics — Worse than anything that has ever happened to a Canadian Politician. Just watch!' The post marked a further escalation in the war of words between the two governments in the days before Canada's Sept 8 retaliatory tariffs take effect, with no new bilateral talks scheduled.

media.caption: Trump warns Carney of consequences for making him 'the enemy' in the trade dispute
